# Questions And Ledger

## One Question At A Time

Ask only a fork that a reasonable user might decide differently and whose answer changes what
ships. Put the recommended option first and explain:

- what each option changes in the deliverable;
- its main benefit;
- its main cost, coupling, or identity risk; and
- the evidence or condition that would reject it.

Keep comparisons symmetric. A coined label is navigation, not an explanation. If a stronger
governing workflow already provides a decision packet, reuse it and add only a missing field.

Use the available question vehicle when it can render the full decision. Otherwise use a
visible prose prompt with the same recommended-first go/veto or option shape. Ask one
independent fork at a time; a tightly coupled sub-decision may share it, and independent
in/out toggles over one surface may use a multi-select.

Give lighter variants their own option. When options differ by an artifact shape, show the
relevant table, fields, configuration, or code preview before ratification. Validate any
computed value in a preview against the authoritative artifact first.

## Rendering And Recovery

Some question tools hide same-turn prose. Put all rationale needed to answer inside the
rendered question/options or in a prior visible turn. When findings or a verdict body are too
large for that surface, deliver them first and ask the fork in the next turn. If the client
cannot initiate another assistant turn without user input, end on the findings; ask the fork
after the user's next message if it remains unresolved.

If a question is unanswered, proceed only with work invariant across the options. After one
soft timeout, take at most one bounded invariant step and carry the fork forward. Repeated
non-response or an explicit away signal permits more invariant work, never a choice on the
user's behalf.

When the user asks for clarification, answer visibly and re-present the same fork. If they
cannot distinguish the options, decline the question call, or report a mis-selection, treat it
as a comprehension reset: infer no decision, rebuild and re-verify the comparison, say if the
recommendation changed, then re-present it. A visible rebuilt comparison may end with its own
prose go/veto prompt.

When the user volunteers answers to several pending branches, accept and record each answer;
do not re-ask them one by one.

## Running Ledger

Record each ratified, evidence-resolved, or derived decision with a stable key, the answer,
its rationale, and its status. In adjudication, the disposition list is the ledger; do not
duplicate it.

For multi-file or multi-phase execution, select or initialize the ledger before the first
mutation. Use the governing process's ledger when it has one; otherwise keep a run-local
scratch ledger unless the repository independently requires persistence. Narration is enough
for short, single-artifact work.

Capture every mid-execution fork when it is taken and before the next mutation. Consecutive
mechanical edits may batch the file write only if the visible narration captured each fork at
the time. Before delivery, sweep the ledger and ensure every mid-execution entry appears once
in the final summary; resolve omissions or extras.

A data-dependent decision may be ratified as a rule with its trigger and premise. Apply it
later only while that premise still holds; a changed premise reopens the fork.

# Recap

Use this before closing an interview or adjudication, accepting blanket approval, or handing
off to execution.

## Closing Recap

After the last fork, restate the ratified decisions, what the deliverable will contain, and
what remains out of scope. A fork answer is not itself the recap.

Scale the checkpoint to consequence:

- For small, reversible work, a separate one-line confirming beat may proceed immediately.
- For large reversible work, name the concrete changes before proceeding.
- For a new consequence that contradicts or reshapes a ratified decision, re-question that
  consequence.
- For hard-to-reverse or outward-facing work such as publishing, deploying, or sending, show
  the concrete action and leave a real veto window before acting.

When the user already saw the exact artifact, confirm that it is unchanged rather than
repeating it. A label-only choice does not count as an artifact preview.

Blanket approval ratifies only a recommendation that was already visible. Do not re-pose that
fork, but still give the scaled recap before execution.

If a self-contained verifier packet is being handed to another executor, the recap also gives
the administrator the acquisition run sheet required by
[Verifier Packets](verification-packets.md); keep blinded material out of the verifier-facing
prompt.

# Execution Contract

Use this before edits, process execution, challenge/retraction handling, or final delivery.

## Before First Mutation

Before mutation, complete in order:

1. Emit the scaled [Recap](recap.md) of ratified scope and exclusions.
2. For multi-file/phase work, select/initialize the
   [running ledger](questions.md#running-ledger).
3. Before product edits, activate the repository implementation workflow and retain its
   pre-edit receipts; if none applies, record why.

Then mutate; keep checkpoints visible in transcript or governing artifact.

## During Execution

Routine mechanics do not erase the ratified boundary. A fork exists when
a reasonable user might choose differently and the choice changes what ships. Mechanical
placement, a reversible label, or illustrative phrasing is not a fork unless inherited as fact.

When new evidence changes a premise, scope, ownership, effect, or deliverable shape, return to
one-question mode. Lead with evidence and recommendation, record the decision, and recap again
before hard-to-reverse work resumes.

A reversible additive choice consistent with ratified decisions may proceed after immediate
ledger capture. A form change may too when substance is preserved; disclose it in the recap.
Adjacent defects stay out of scope unless mechanically required, cheap, additive, and
reversible; otherwise ask or defer. Capture every qualifying fork before the next mutation and
sweep the ledger into the final summary.

## Sub-Processes And Gates

When an invoked sub-process owns a user-facing approval gate, give it the ratified inputs and
let that gate serve as the single checkpoint. Do not add a duplicate confirmation or suppress
the sub-process's gate.

When the current thread executes the sub-process directly, present its recap here. If a named
workflow is unavailable but its repository contract is readable, disclose the fallback,
follow the contract, and preserve its gates. Without a readable contract or sufficient
authority, stop at the narrowest safe handoff.

## Retractions And Challenges

If the user retracts a ratified item, keep unaffected items ratified and rework only that item
and its dependents. If the user challenges the result's accuracy or completeness, re-check the
challenged claim against the ratified scope, correct the artifact and framing, and disclose
the correction. Do not restart the whole interview unless the rationale invalidates the rest.

## Final Reconciliation

Before delivery:

1. Restate what the recap put in and out of scope.
2. Reconcile the actual diff or deliverable with that boundary.
3. Sweep mid-execution forks from the ledger into the summary.
4. Scope words such as complete, full, or done to the ratified deliverable.
5. Run the repository's completion/landing contract. For a structured landing, read it before
   editing as well as at closeout.

## Artifact-Specific Closeout

For a non-product durable artifact such as a skill, template, or process document, name the
artifact class and why it was in scope, include a literal provenance line naming the evidence
that justified it, state the convention checked, and report any applicable mirror, pointer,
formatter, validator, or equivalent proof.

When a companion domain workflow was used, include a domain-doc outcome line for every
glossary or ADR surface it requires, naming the update or saying none was needed and citing
the evidence for that disposition.
